name: Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young Type 3 (HNF1A-MODY)

clinicalPearls: Caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in HNF1A and is the most common form of MODY in many populations; inheritance is autosomal dominant with high, age-dependent penetrance.
Presents typically in adolescence or young adulthood with progressive hyperglycaemia and a striking sensitivity to low-dose sulfonylureas, which are the preferred first-line therapy.
A characteristic low renal threshold for glucose causes glycosuria at near-normal or only mildly elevated blood glucose, an important diagnostic clue.
The oral glucose tolerance test often shows a large glucose increment, contrasting with the small increment of GCK-MODY.
Highly sensitive C-reactive protein tends to be low in HNF1A-MODY, a feature that can help discriminate it from type 2 diabetes.
Diabetes is progressive: beta-cell function declines over years and some patients ultimately need insulin despite an initial sulfonylurea response.
Microvascular and macrovascular complications occur at rates comparable to other diabetes, so good glycaemic control remains important.
Consider the diagnosis in young, lean, autoantibody-negative, C-peptide-positive patients with a strong multigenerational family history of diabetes.
reference.pathophysiology: MODY3 is caused by heterozygous inactivating mutations in HNF1A, encoding hepatocyte nuclear factor 1-alpha, a transcription factor that regulates the expression of numerous genes essential for beta-cell development and function, including those controlling glucose transport, mitochondrial metabolism and insulin gene expression. Haploinsufficiency, sometimes compounded by a dominant-negative effect, leads to progressive failure of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion; beta-cell function is often near-normal in childhood but deteriorates through adolescence and adult life, producing worsening hyperglycaemia. HNF1A is also expressed in the renal proximal tubule where it drives expression of the sodium-glucose co-transporter, so mutation lowers the renal threshold for glucose and produces glycosuria disproportionate to the blood glucose. The transcription factor additionally influences hepatic synthesis of C-reactive protein and certain lipids, accounting for the characteristically low high-sensitivity CRP and altered lipid pattern. Residual beta cells retain a functional KATP-channel pathway, which explains their pronounced responsiveness to sulfonylureas that close this channel and augment insulin release, often at doses far lower than used in type 2 diabetes.
additionalDifferentials: HNF4A-MODY (MODY1), which is closely similar but has a normal renal glucose threshold and neonatal macrosomia
Type 1 diabetes mellitus (autoantibody positive, low C-peptide)
Young-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus with obesity and insulin resistance
Glucokinase-MODY (MODY2) with mild stable fasting hyperglycaemia and small OGTT increment
Renal glycosuria from SGLT2 (SLC5A2) mutations when glycosuria is the dominant finding
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of HNF1A (sequencing and dosage), usually within a MODY gene panel
Pancreatic islet autoantibodies (GAD, IA-2, ZnT8) to exclude type 1 diabetes
Fasting and stimulated C-peptide to confirm preserved endogenous insulin secretion
Urinalysis for glycosuria relative to concurrent blood glucose
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein, which is characteristically low
Oral glucose tolerance test to demonstrate a large glucose increment
Three-generation family pedigree documenting autosomal dominant diabetes
redFlags: Progressive loss of glycaemic control indicating declining beta-cell reserve and possible need for insulin
Emergence of retinopathy, nephropathy or neuropathy, since complication risk is substantial
Recurrent hypoglycaemia after starting sulfonylurea, reflecting the exquisite drug sensitivity and need for careful dose titration
Diabetic ketoacidosis, which should prompt reassessment for type 1 diabetes
Pregnancy, requiring specialist review of therapy and glycaemic targets
reference.prognosis: The diabetes is progressive, but genetic diagnosis allows a shift from insulin to low-dose sulfonylurea in many patients with durable benefit for years; beta-cell function nonetheless declines and some ultimately need insulin. Long-term outcome depends on glycaemic control because complication risk is comparable to other diabetes.
pitfalls: Labelling the patient as type 1 diabetes and using unnecessary insulin when sulfonylurea would achieve control
Starting a standard rather than a low sulfonylurea approach and precipitating hypoglycaemia due to marked drug sensitivity
Misclassifying as type 2 diabetes and missing the opportunity for targeted therapy and family testing
Overlooking glycosuria out of proportion to blood glucose as a diagnostic pointer
Assuming benign non-progressive disease and neglecting complication screening
